subject: Business
title: Psychological Safety in Teams
description: Learn Psychological Safety in Teams in one minute.

hook.text: Google studied its best teams for two years. The top factor wasn't talent or experience. It was psychological safety.

buildup.text: Psychological safety means team members feel safe to take risks, ask questions, and admit mistakes.

discovery.text: In safe teams, errors are reported early. In unsafe ones, they're hidden — until they become catastrophes.

twist.text: High-performing teams have more reported errors, not fewer. They just catch and fix them faster.

climax.text: Amy Edmondson found hospitals with better error reporting had lower patient mortality. Safety saves lives.

punchline.text: The best teams aren't fearless. They're safe enough to be honest.

quiz.question: What was the number one factor in Google's highest-performing teams?

details.summary: Psychological safety, coined by Amy Edmondson, is a team climate where people feel safe to take interpersonal risks like admitting mistakes, asking questions, and challenging ideas without fear of punishment or humiliation.
details.whyItMatters: Without psychological safety, teams cannot learn from mistakes, raise concerns early, or innovate through experimentation. Google found it was more predictive of team performance than individual talent, structure, or any other measured factor.
takeaways: Psychological safety means feeling safe to take interpersonal risks at work
Google found it is the number one predictor of team effectiveness over talent
Leaders create safety by responding well to bad news and admitting their own errors

faq.question: How can a leader build psychological safety in their team?
faq.answer: Admit your own mistakes openly. Thank people who raise problems or disagree. Respond to bad news with curiosity rather than anger. Frame failures as learning opportunities. Ask questions to show vulnerability. Ensure people who speak up are never punished for their honesty.

faq.question: Does psychological safety mean avoiding accountability?
faq.answer: Absolutely not. Edmondson emphasizes that psychological safety and high standards must coexist. Safety means you can admit errors, ask for help, and challenge ideas. Accountability means you are still expected to perform. The combination produces learning organizations that continuously improve.
